## 2. Historical evidence and institutional constraints

The official Nobel-data query covered **2000–2025 inclusive: 26 annual Medicine prizes and 63 laureates**, from the October 9, 2000 announcement through the October 6, 2025 announcement. Using the published motivations, I classified those 26 prizes as follows. These are my descriptive categories, not official Nobel classifications:

| Broad category | Prize years | Count |
|---|---|---:|
| Basic cellular or molecular biology | 2001, 2002, 2006, 2007, 2009, 2012, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2024 | 10 |
| Neuroscience, sensory biology, or circadian physiology | 2000, 2004, 2014, 2017, 2021 | 5 |
| Clinical therapy or medical technology | 2003, 2010, 2015, 2018, 2023 | 5 |
| Infection or immunity | 2005, 2008, 2011, 2020, 2025 | 5 |
| Human evolution | 2022 | 1 |

The principal lesson is that clinical translation is helpful but not required: basic cellular biology accounts for 10/26 prizes in this classification. I did not mechanically apply these proportions to the candidate list, because category boundaries are subjective and the underlying eligible-discovery pool is unknown. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/all-nobel-laureates-in-physiology-or-medicine/?utm_source=openai))

Precursor prizes establish scientific stature much better than they establish the precise year of Nobel recognition. For example, Ambros and Ruvkun received a Lasker award in 2008 and the Medicine Nobel in 2024, a 16-year gap. This is an illustrative historical example, not an estimated conversion rate. It argues against discarding mature candidates simply because their recognition is old—and against assuming that the newest Lasker winner must win immediately. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/rnas-extreme-makeover/?utm_source=openai))

Institutional timing reinforces that restraint. The Nobel Foundation describes expert assessment during February–August, recommendations in September, and selection and announcement in October. Nomination and evaluation documents remain confidential for 50 years. I therefore interpret September awards as evidence of scientific consensus and current salience, not as evidence of access to the Nobel shortlist or a last-minute causal influence on the selection. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2025/04/annual-review-2024.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## 3. Evidence for the leading discoveries

### GLP-1: strongest accumulated discovery-to-therapy case

The **2024 Lasker Clinical award** recognized Habener, Mojsov, and Knudsen for GLP-1-based obesity therapies. The **2025 Breakthrough Prize**, announced April 5, 2025, recognized Drucker, Habener, Holst, Knudsen, and Mojsov for the broader discovery, physiological characterization, and therapeutic-development chain. Together, these provide strong independent recognition that the achievement is suitable for a discovery-level medical prize. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/glp-1-based-therapy-for-obesity/))

There is also a genuinely current signal: **Clarivate's September 17, 2026 Citation Laureates announcement** recognized Drucker, Holst, and Mojsov for GLP-1 identification, characterization, and biological activity. I give this less weight than a Nobel decision or a clinical outcome, but it is additional contemporary expert recognition. Importantly, it means GLP-1 is not competing solely on a two-year-old publicity wave. ([clarivate.com](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-reveals-citation-laureates-2026-recognizing-transformative-scientific-breakthroughs/?utm_source=openai))

The medical significance extends beyond weight reduction. On **March 8, 2024**, FDA approved a semaglutide indication for reducing cardiovascular death, heart attack, and stroke in adults with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity. That supports a durable health-benefit narrative rather than one resting only on commercial success or cosmetic weight loss. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-treatment-reduce-risk-serious-heart-problems-specifically-adults-obesity-or))

My main reservations are selection timing and attribution. The five-person Breakthrough recognition illustrates a crowded discovery-to-treatment history. However, I apply only a modest allocation penalty because this question does not require a particular trio. Habener died on **December 28, 2025**, according to the National Academy of Sciences; this changes possible recipient combinations, but does not eliminate the GLP-1 discovery from consideration. I do not treat his death as a categorical obstacle to recognition of the surviving contributors. ([breakthroughprize.org](https://breakthroughprize.org/News/91))

**Assessment:** GLP-1 has the strongest combination of established physiology, substantial demonstrated medical benefit, accumulated recognition, and current visibility. It leads among individual listed discoveries, but those strengths do not tell us whether the Assembly will choose it specifically in 2026.

### Orexin: largest fresh upward revision

The **2026 Lasker Basic award**, announced September 9, honored Mignot and Yanagisawa for identifying orexin's role in wakefulness and showing that orexin deficiency causes narcolepsy. The underlying peptide discoveries date to 1998, with decisive animal-genetic disease links in 1999. This is therefore a mature fundamental-physiology discovery, not an immature therapeutic fashion. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/awards/media-center/))

On **August 5, 2026**, FDA approved **Orzeyful, or oveporexton**, for adults with narcolepsy type 1. FDA describes it as directly restoring orexin signaling. Its approval evidence included **two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies, each lasting 12 weeks, enrolling 273 adults in total**. Those are participant counts and study durations, not annual treatment-use figures. The announcement does not provide the studies' calendar enrollment windows, so I do not imply that the trials themselves occurred in August 2026. The regulatory vintage is the dated August 5 announcement. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-drug-treat-full-range-narcolepsy-type-1-symptoms))

This gives orexin a particularly clear chain: discovery of a physiological signal, explanation of a disease mechanism, and intervention on that same mechanism. That combination warrants a much larger update than another honorary award alone.

There are counterweights. FDA describes the treated disorder as rare, whereas GLP-1's medical applications are broader. FDA approval also did not establish immediate unrestricted commercial availability: the announcement said marketing would follow DEA scheduling. More importantly for this forecast, a fresh Lasker award is not proof of same-season Nobel selection. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-drug-treat-full-range-narcolepsy-type-1-symptoms))

**Assessment:** orexin moves from a secondary candidate to a strong challenger. The specialist reports favored it over GLP-1, but I retain GLP-1 as the individual leader because I give greater weight to accumulated recognition and breadth of demonstrated benefit, and less weight to the apparent immediacy of the Lasker timing.

Lifetime output, reviews, patents, textbook exposure, and co-authorship are also different quantities from the importance and attribution of the particular discovery being considered.

Without an exclusion rule, that discrepancy is unresolved. Several reported publication windows also begin as early as 1889 or 1924, warranting author-identity checks before using the associated counts. ## 7. Reproducible probability calculation

I used an explicit **judgmental weighting model**, not a fitted statistical model. Its inputs are subjective and should not be mistaken for empirically estimated likelihood ratios.

First, I elicited a durable-record distribution, **b**, using scientific importance, established recognition, Medicine-category fit, and discovery-level attribution. This component excludes the specifically itemized fresh signals used for the update. It reserves 30% for Other and gives GLP-1 the largest individual baseline.

Second, I applied relative evidence multipliers, **m**. Orexin receives the largest multiplier for the conjunction of the new Lasker recognition and direct mechanism-based FDA approval. GLP-1 receives a smaller multiplier because its baseline already reflects strong established recognition, with the 2026 Clarivate signal adding current evidence. The CAR-T, PCSK9, sequencing, and leptin updates are more modest. Other gets a small positive update for the fresh omitted-discovery evidence.

Third, I normalized the updated weights and blended them with the durable-record component:

**u_i = b_i × m_i / Σ(b_j × m_j)**

**p_i = 0.85 × u_i + 0.15 × b_i**

The 15% durable-record blend is a judgmental safeguard against overinterpreting seasonal recognition. It is not a parameter estimated from historical data.

|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GLP-1 | 0.190 | 1.60 | 22.1805 |
| Optogenetics | 0.100 | 1.00 | 7.8587 |
| CAR-T | 0.070 | 1.15 | 6.1688 |
| Unfolded protein response | 0.065 | 1.00 | 5.1082 |
| PCSK9 | 0.035 | 1.40 | 3.6408 |

| Orexin | 0.050 | 4.50 | 15.0571 |

Python calculation gives **Σ(b_j × m_j) = 1.33675**. I rounded the final probabilities to six decimal places using largest-remainder allocation, ensuring an exact decimal total of **1.000000**.

## 8. Sensitivity and confidence

The principal uncertainty is not whether these discoveries are important; it is which one the confidential selection process will recognize this year.

One-input-at-a-time sensitivity checks illustrate that uncertainty:

- Changing GLP-1's multiplier from 1.2 to 2.0 moves its probability from approximately **18.22% to 25.71%**.
- Changing orexin's multiplier from 2.5 to 6.5 moves its probability from approximately **9.34% to 19.98%**.
- Changing the baseline Other reserve from 20% to 40%, while proportionally rescaling listed baselines, moves final Other from approximately **15.96% to 33.55%**.

These are model-sensitivity ranges, **not statistical confidence intervals**, and simultaneous changes could produce wider ranges. The six decimal places document the calculation and preserve normalization; they do not imply that the underlying probabilities are known to millionth-level accuracy. My substantive conclusion is a diffuse distribution: GLP-1 leads individually, orexin has the strongest fresh upward signal, and omitted discoveries collectively remain highly competitive.

## 1. Interpretation of the resolution criteria

I forecast the **discovery selected by the official motivation**, not an exact combination of laureates. Consequently:

- A GLP-1 award could match even if Daniel Drucker were a recipient instead of one of the three people in the option.
- An optogenetics award could match with a different set of contributors.
- An orexin award could match if only Mignot and Yanagisawa were honored.
- If two discoveries receive equal aggregate shares, I apply the client's rule that the discovery named first counts. I do not use the order of scientists in the option labels.

Discovery boundaries still matter. A prize for pharmacological stabilization of transthyretin would not automatically be the chaperone-mediated folding option. Likewise, Notch signaling is not Wnt signaling; gene replacement or base editing is not next-generation sequencing; and an award specifically for tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes would not automatically match CAR-T. I allow some residual uncertainty about broad or compound motivations in the Other allocation.

The official nomination information is confidential for 50 years. Public awards and scientific achievements therefore establish plausibility and readiness, but do not reveal the actual 2026 shortlist or committee preferences. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/nomination/archive/?trk=public_post_comment-text&utm_source=openai))

## 2. Research approach and the decision-relevant questions

I investigated three principal questions that could materially change the ranking:

1. **What changed recently?** In particular, did any candidate acquire a new major award or decisive clinical validation during 2025–2026?
2. **Which discoveries fit this particular Nobel category?** I examined the distinction between biological protein-folding machinery and the 2024 Chemistry prize, and the possibility that sequencing would be recognized in Chemistry rather than Medicine.
3. **How complete is the supplied list?** I examined recent Lasker, Breakthrough, Gairdner, Shaw, and Kavli recognition for strong omitted discoveries rather than assuming that twelve named options captured almost all probability.

The evidence base combines official Nobel records, the prize foundations' own announcements, FDA releases, and primary institutional reporting. I also used the Nobel-data MCP for the 2000–2025 award record and the news MCP for a date-bounded check of September 2026 coverage. Two parallel research reports checked recent prize flows and scientific/category readiness, and a separate historical audit checked Nobel–Lasker overlap. The final weights are my synthesis of the underlying evidence, not an average of those reports' suggested probabilities.

The largest positive update was to **orexin**, after verifying both its September 2026 Lasker recognition and the August 2026 FDA approval of a mechanism-restoring treatment. A systematic search of omitted discoveries also increased my Other reserve from an initial 25% to 28%. The evidence for those updates is detailed below.

## 3. Historical calibration: major awards help, but immediate succession is uncommon

I reconstructed a prize-year-level audit covering **26 Nobel Medicine announcements, from October 9, 2000, through October 6, 2025**, comprising **63 laureates**. For each year, the audit asked whether at least one eventual laureate had already received a Lasker Basic or Clinical award before the Nobel announcement. Special Achievement awards were distinguished from Basic and Clinical awards. The source records are the official Nobel history and Lasker archives. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/laureates/?utm_source=openai))

The results, calculated from historical award records available by the forecast cutoff, are:

| Indicator | Nobel prize years | Proportion |
|---|---:|---:|
| At least one laureate with an earlier Lasker Basic/Clinical award | 18/26 | 69.2308% |
| A qualifying Lasker earlier in the same calendar year | 1/26 | 3.8462% |
| A qualifying Lasker within two calendar years, including same-year | 2/26 | 7.6923% |
| A qualifying Lasker within five calendar years, including same-year | 10/26 | 38.4615% |

For reproducibility, the most recent qualifying Lasker years in the 18 overlapping Nobel years were: **2000→1983; 2001→1998; 2002→1971; 2003→1984; 2005→1995; 2007→2001; 2008→1986; 2009→2006; 2010→2001; 2011→2007; 2012→2009; 2013→2013; 2015→2011; 2018→2015; 2019→2016; 2020→2016; 2023→2021; 2024→2008**. These are person-overlap indicators; some Lasker motivations cover a different or broader aspect of the laureate's research. They are not all exact matches to this question's primary-discovery rule. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/laureates/?utm_source=openai))

The same-year case was Thomas Südhof in 2013: the Lasker announcement preceded that year's Nobel announcement. The Lasker press release is dated September 9, 2013. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/2013_awrads_press_release.pdf))

**The crucial statistical limitation is that these are estimates of P(prior Lasker recognition | eventual Nobel), not P(Nobel this year | Lasker recognition).** Reversing the conditional would require the denominator of all eligible Lasker-winning discoveries that did not subsequently win. The small same-year count also cautions against treating September 2026's Lasker award as a near-certain precursor to October 2026's Nobel.

My takeaway is therefore two-sided: major-prize corroboration deserves substantial weight, but older Lasker winners remain competitive, and a recent Lasker does not by itself identify the next Nobel winner.

The medical case is not simply commercial popularity or weight loss. FDA's **March 8, 2024** announcement expanded semaglutide's indication to reducing serious cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity. I treat that as additional validation of substantial medical benefit, rather than using sales or citation counts as a proxy for Nobel merit. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-treatment-reduce-risk-serious-heart-problems-specifically-adults-obesity-or?utm_source=openai))

The 2025 Breakthrough award credited five contributors, while Nobel prizes can be shared by at most three people. **Forecast judgment:** GLP-1 is my leading named option because its natural citation combines fundamental endocrinology with exceptionally consequential therapy. ### Orexin: the strongest recent positive development

The Lasker Foundation announced on **September 9, 2026** that Mignot and Yanagisawa would receive the Basic Medical Research award for identifying orexin's role in maintaining wakefulness and establishing that its deficiency causes narcolepsy. They had also received the **2023 Breakthrough Prize**, announced on **September 22, 2022**. The award-year/announcement-year distinction matters when assessing recency. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026-press-release2.pdf))

I use the FDA announcement as clinical validation; I do not equate approval with unrestricted commercial availability or claim that the disease is cured. The recognition events are correlated indicators of the same achievement, not independent likelihood multipliers, and their late timing does not prove that they changed the Nobel deliberations. The Nobel institution's historical account describes repeated evaluation of leading candidates over multiple years, with expert reports completed before the autumn announcement. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/chaperone-assisted-protein-folding/))

The **2024 Chemistry Nobel**, announced October 9, 2024, recognized computational protein design and protein-structure prediction. Those are not the same discovery as cellular machinery that assists folding. I therefore reject the strong version of the crowding-out argument—that protein folding has already been awarded and this option is effectively ineligible. Any weaker thematic-crowding effect is uncertain and not grounds for a large numerical penalty. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2024/press-release/?trk=public_post-text&utm_source=openai))

**Forecast judgment:** the clean mechanism, mature evidence, and repeated recognition justify a substantial 7.088% allocation despite the absence of a new 2026 catalyst.

### Unfolded protein response: a similarly credible basic-physiology choice

Mori and Walter received the **2014 Lasker Basic award** for an intracellular system that senses harmful unfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum and activates corrective responses. The **2018 Breakthrough recognition** provides additional corroboration. This is distinct from both chaperone-assisted folding and computational structure prediction. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/unfolded-protein-response/))

**Forecast judgment:** UPR's generality, mechanistic clarity, and compact attribution make it a serious candidate. I give it 5.906%, below chaperones but above CAR-T. I do not require a new clinical approval for it to win; I simply find less new evidence to increase its weight this year.

### CAR-T: transformative medicine with renewed recognition

The **2024 Breakthrough Prize** recognized CAR-T development. June and Sadelain also received the BBVA Frontiers of Knowledge recognition announced on **February 11, 2026**, for pioneering genetically engineered T-cell treatments. This strengthens an already substantial therapeutic case. ([breakthroughprize.org](https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/2/L3952))

The **2025 Medicine Nobel**, announced October 6, 2025, honored peripheral immune tolerance. That is not CAR-T and does not remove CAR-T from the candidate pool. I do not impose a mechanical rule that immunology cannot win in consecutive years; any committee preference for thematic variety is speculative. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2025/press-release/%26nbsp/?utm_source=openai))

**Forecast judgment:** CAR-T receives 5.434%. Its current awards improve its standing, but I do not regard its clinical importance as evidence that it must outrank foundational discoveries this particular year.

## 5. The remaining named options

| Discovery | Verified evidence and forecast implication |
|---|---|
| **PCSK9** | FDA's release dated **July 17, 2026** reported approval of the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor, enlicitide. This is a meaningful new translation signal, but an additional delivery format is a smaller readiness change than the first direct restoration of orexin signaling. I apply a modest positive adjustment. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-oral-pcsk9-inhibitor-lower-ldl-cholesterol-adults-high-cholesterol)) |
| **Wnt/organoids** | Clevers' **2013 Breakthrough citation** recognized Wnt signaling in tissue stem cells and cancer. This supports a strong basic-biological case. I retain roughly 4%, while allowing for uncertainty over whether a potential stem-cell/organoid motivation would match this compound option's discovery boundary. ([breakthroughprize.org](https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/2/L29?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Next-generation sequencing** | Klenerman, Balasubramanian, and Mayer received the **2026 Princess of Asturias scientific-research award**, with the jury decision dated **May 13, 2026**. The importance is unquestionable, but category fit is a significant discount: sequencing methods have a Chemistry precedent in the **1980 Nobel**. That precedent does not exclude modern NGS from Medicine; it lowers the probability of this particular prize being its home. ([fpa.es](https://www.fpa.es/en/princess-of-asturias-awards/laureates/2026-david-klenerman-shankar-balasubramanian-pascal-mayer/?texto=acta&utm_source=openai)) |
| **BRCA/inherited cancer susceptibility** | King's **2014 Lasker Special Achievement citation** explicitly recognized her discovery of the hereditary breast-cancer locus. That is supporting evidence, but a career-wide Special Achievement award is not directly interchangeable with a discovery-specific Basic or Clinical award. I retain a meaningful long-shot allocation. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/2014-lasker-awards-winners/)) |
| **Leptin** | The **2010 Lasker Basic award** recognized Coleman and Friedman for the hormone regulating appetite and body weight. The discovery remains fundamental. My relative discount reflects competition within metabolic physiology, especially the more recently validated GLP-1 discovery-to-treatment narrative—not a judgment that leptin was unimportant. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/leptin-a-hormone-that-regulates-appetite-and-body-weight/)) |
| **Anti-TNF** | The **2003 Lasker Clinical award** recognized Feldmann and Maini for anti-TNF treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases. This is an established, consequential medical achievement. I assign less weight to an immediate 2026 selection because I found less new evidence to distinguish it from the many other mature candidates. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/anti-tnf-for-treating-rheumatoid-arthritis/)) |

## 6. Why Other receives 28%, rather than a token residual

The supplied list is strong, but a recent-prize sweep demonstrates substantial omitted competition:

- **cGAS-mediated DNA sensing:** the 2024 Lasker Basic award recognized James Chen's discovery explaining how self and foreign DNA trigger immune and inflammatory responses. This is a focused, Medicine-fitting omitted discovery. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/cgas-enzyme-that-senses-self-and-foreign-dna/))
- **CFTR biology and cystic-fibrosis therapy:** Welsh and Negulescu received Gairdner recognition announced **April 11, 2025**, followed by the **2025 Lasker Clinical award** for triple-drug therapy. The same Lasker announcement also honored low-complexity protein domains and cellular organization through Görlich and McKnight. These are not automatic matches to the listed chaperone option. ([gairdner.org](https://www.gairdner.org/resource-hub/2025-canada-gairdner-award-winners))
- **Cryo-electron tomography, tafamidis, and systems proteomics:** these were recognized in the **2026 Gairdner announcement**, whose page header is dated **March 31, 2026**. Cryo-ET and proteomics have category-boundary uncertainty, but they broaden the omitted pool. ([gairdner.org](https://www.gairdner.org/resource-hub/2026-canada-gairdner-award-winners))
- **Inherited-retinal-disease gene replacement, fetal-to-adult hemoglobin switching, and C9orf72-related ALS/frontotemporal dementia:** all appeared in the **April 18, 2026 Breakthrough announcement**. A hemoglobin-switching prize, for example, would be distinct from a prize for genome-editing chemistry or sequencing. ([breakthroughprize.org](https://breakthroughprize.org/News/98))
- **Acute promyelocytic leukemia and synergistic targeted treatment:** the **May 27, 2026 Shaw announcement** recognized Dejean, de Thé, and Zhu Chen. ([prnewswire.com](https://www.prnewswire.com/in/news-releases/announcement-of-the-shaw-laureates-2026-302782961.html))
- **Local protein translation in neurons:** the **2026 Kavli Neuroscience award** recognized Holt, Martin, Schuman, and Steward. This demonstrates that the neuroscience alternatives are not limited to orexin and optogenetics. ([kavliprize.org](https://www.kavliprize.org/prizes/neuroscience/2026))

These awards are not independent votes and should not be counted mechanically. Some recognize the same discovery more than once, while the named options possess older recognition outside a narrow recent window. Nevertheless, the omitted pool is sufficiently broad that I would be uncomfortable putting Other below approximately one fifth.

I use **28% as a central judgment**, between a concentrated-shortlist scenario at 20% and a broader omitted-pool scenario at 36%. Those endpoints are sensitivity assumptions, not a statistically estimated confidence interval. Other is the largest category because it combines many alternatives; I am not claiming that one particular omitted discovery has a 28% chance.

## 7. Treatment of the supplied bibliometric profiles

I did not fit a regression or assign probabilities directly from the supplied percentiles. The profiles lack the author identifiers and underlying work-level records needed for an independent audit, and several features need reconciliation:

- Publication ranges such as **1889–2021 for Feldmann** and **1924–2021 for Holst** span 132 and 97 years respectively. They are warning signs for possible author-identity contamination or other metadata problems.
- The stated benchmark contains 60 Medicine laureates for 2000–2025, whereas the official award record contains 63 laureates across those years. An unstated exclusion could explain the difference, so I do not assert that every benchmark statistic is wrong; the denominator needs clarification before modeling. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/laureates/?utm_source=openai))
- A person's most-cited work can be a review, an adjacent contribution, or a paper unrelated to the discovery in the option. Career-level impact is not the same outcome as selection of a particular discovery.
- The profiles compare candidate records through 2021 with laureate records measured before their prizes. That is not a uniformly matched observation window, and there is no supplied nonwinner comparison group from which to estimate annual selection probabilities.

Accordingly, the profiles help identify established researchers, but I assign **no direct numerical coefficient** to citations, patents, disruption percentiles, textbook reach, or Nobel co-authorship. Verified discoveries, prize citations, clinical validation, and category fit drive the weights instead.

## 8. Numerical construction

I use transparent **relative selection weights**, with an explicit Other reserve. The baseline scores summarize my judgment of scientific importance, maturity, and established recognition. The multipliers summarize the net current-evidence and category-fit adjustments discussed above. Neither set is an empirically estimated coefficient.

| Discovery | Baseline score | Net multiplier | Final weight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GLP-1 | 18 | 1.40 | 25.20 |
| Optogenetics | 13 | 1.05 | 13.65 |
| CAR-T | 8 | 1.15 | 9.20 |
| UPR | 10 | 1.00 | 10.00 |
| PCSK9 | 6 | 1.10 | 6.60 |
| NGS | 8 | 0.55 | 4.40 |
| Orexin | 9 | 2.50 | 22.50 |
| Wnt/organoids | 7 | 0.95 | 6.65 |
| Leptin | 5 | 0.80 | 4.00 |
| Anti-TNF | 4 | 0.80 | 3.20 |
| Chaperone-mediated folding | 12 | 1.00 | 12.00 |
| BRCA | 5 | 0.90 | 4.50 |

The weights sum to **121.90**. With Other fixed at 0.28, the listed discoveries collectively receive 0.72. For each listed discovery i, I calculate:

**P(i) = 0.72 × final_weight(i) / 121.90.**

For example, **P(GLP-1) = 0.72 × 25.20 / 121.90 = 0.1488433142**, while **P(orexin) = 0.72 × 22.50 / 121.90 = 0.1328958162**. Python decimal arithmetic produced the final probabilities. Rounding each to five decimal places leaves the total exactly **1.00000**, without assigning a rounding residual to any option.

The multiplier of 2.50 for orexin is a judgmental net adjustment for its unusually strong verified convergence of discovery recognition and clinical validation. It is deliberately not the product of separate independent likelihood ratios for Lasker, Breakthrough, and FDA approval. The NGS multiplier of 0.55 is predominantly a category discount, not a scientific-merit discount. The small reductions for several older candidates reflect relative competition and citation-boundary uncertainty, not a rule that mature discoveries expire.

## 9. Sensitivity, limitations, and confidence

The model makes the main uncertainties auditable:

- Holding named-option weights fixed but changing Other from **20% to 36%** moves GLP-1 from **16.538% to 13.231%**, and orexin from **14.766% to 11.813%**.
- Holding Other at 28% but changing orexin's multiplier from **2.00 to 3.00** moves orexin from **11.039% to 15.380%**. At the upper setting, it overtakes GLP-1, which falls to **14.354%** after renormalization.
- Thus, the narrow GLP-1 lead is not robust enough to justify a confident winner prediction.

A further data-quality check concerns publication dates. Historical award pages often display site-migration timestamps rather than original announcement dates, so I use the award year and original releases where available. The 2026 Gairdner page also contains an inconsistent year in its introductory text; its header, title, and award descriptions identify 2026. I use March 31, 2026 as the announcement date and flag the inconsistency rather than silently treating the body text as a different vintage. ([gairdner.org](https://www.gairdner.org/resource-hub/2026-canada-gairdner-award-winners))

Finally, I have no verified information about live nominations, deliberations, or an inside shortlist. The short time to announcement reduces the scope for new scientific developments to matter, but does not reduce uncertainty about the private decision. I did not consult or use prediction-market prices, betting odds, or public probability aggregates.

**Bottom line:** GLP-1 has the strongest overall named discovery-to-medical-benefit case; orexin has the strongest verified recent improvement in Nobel readiness; optogenetics and the protein-quality-control discoveries remain credible alternatives. The breadth of omitted discoveries justifies retaining 28% for Other rather than concentrating the forecast around a fashionable single candidate.

write_up:
## TL;DR

Other is the largest resolution category at 32.9%. GLP-1 leads the named discoveries at 18%, followed by orexin at 12%. The list omits established contenders with major precursor awards, so this is not a two-discovery race ([Lasker: optical coherence tomography](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/optical-coherence-tomography/), [Japan Prize: nucleic-acid sensing](https://www.japanprize.jp/en/prize_past_2026_prize02.html)).

## Context

This forecast uses the client's cutoff of October 2, 2026, at 14:21 UTC. The Medicine announcement is scheduled for October 5 at 11:30 CEST at the earliest, or 09:30 UTC—67 hours and nine minutes after that cutoff ([official schedule](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/about/prize-announcement-dates/)). The resolving event is the forthcoming award announcement, even though the discoveries being considered can be decades old.

I match the discovery, not the exact laureate roster, and apply the client's larger-share/first-mentioned rule. Public awards reveal scientific standing, not a verified Nobel shortlist. The committee prepares its recommendation during the summer and presents it in September; nominations and evaluations remain confidential for 50 years ([Nobel Foundation annual review](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2025/04/annual-review-2024.pdf)).

## Evidence

The historical backbone supports using precursor prizes to identify serious candidates, but not to predict the immediate winning year. Across all 16 completed Medicine Nobel prize-years from 2010 through 2025, ten included a discovery substantially overlapping an earlier or same-year Lasker Basic or Clinical research award. The unit is a Nobel prize-year, not a person; Special Achievement and Public Service awards are excluded. These are retrospective counts from official historical records available at the forecast cutoff ([Nobel records](https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/nobelPrizes?nobelPrizeYear=2010&yearTo=2025&nobelPrizeCategory=med&limit=100), [Lasker archive](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/)).

| Nobel year | Qualifying Lasker research award year | Match survives this question's discovery-selection rule? |
|---|---|---|
| [2010](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2010/summary/) | [2001: IVF](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/in-vitro-fertilization-for-treating-infertility/) | Yes |
| [2011](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2011/press-release/) | [2007: dendritic cells](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/dendritic-cells-and-the-immune-response/) | No: equal-share discovery listed second |
| [2012](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2012/summary/) | [2009: cellular reprogramming](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/nuclear-reprogramming-converting-specialized-cells-into-early-stem-cells/) | Yes |
| [2013](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2013/summary/) | [2002: membrane fusion](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/membrane-fusion-and-organelle-formation/); [2013: neurotransmitter release](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/regulated-neurotransmitter-release/) | Yes |
| [2014](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2014/summary/) | No qualifying match identified | No |
| [2015](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2015/press-release/) | [2011: artemisinin](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/artemisinin-therapy-for-malaria/) | No: equal-share discovery listed second |
| [2016](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2016/summary/) | No qualifying match identified | No |
| [2017](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2017/summary/) | No qualifying match identified | No |
| [2018](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2018/summary/) | [2015: checkpoint cancer therapy](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/unleashing-the-immune-system-to-combat-cancer/) | Yes |
| [2019](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2019/summary/) | [2016: oxygen sensing](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/oxygen-sensing-an-essential-process-for-survival/) | Yes |
| [2020](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2020/summary/) | [2000: hepatitis C](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/hepatitis-c-virus-and-its-detection-in-blood-for-transfusions/) | Yes |
| [2021](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2021/summary/) | No qualifying match identified | No |
| [2022](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2022/summary/) | No qualifying match identified | No |
| [2023](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2023/summary/) | [2021: modified mRNA](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/modified-mrna-vaccines/) | Yes |
| [2024](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2024/summary/) | [2008: small regulatory RNAs](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/tiny-rnas-that-regulate-gene-function/) | Yes |
| [2025](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2025/summary/) | No qualifying match identified | No |

Applying the client's rule reduces the overlap from ten to eight prize-years. Only one prize-year had a same-calendar-year Lasker match: Südhof's neurotransmitter-release work in 2013 ([Lasker record](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/regulated-neurotransmitter-release/), [Nobel record](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2013/summary/)). Neither count estimates the chance that a particular Lasker winner wins this year's Nobel. Selecting Nobel winners first reverses the forecasting denominator.

GLP-1 has the strongest named case across scientific importance, medical translation, and repeated recognition. Its award sequence includes the 2024 Lasker Clinical prize, the 2025 Breakthrough Prize announced on April 5, 2025, and Clarivate recognition on September 17, 2026. The organizations recognized different contributor groups, but the discovery-development chain remains coherent ([Lasker](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/glp-1-based-therapy-for-obesity/), [Breakthrough](https://breakthroughprize.org/News/91), [Clarivate](https://ir.clarivate.com/news-events/press-releases/news-details/2026/Clarivate-Reveals-Citation-Laureates-2026-Recognizing-Transformative-Scientific-Breakthroughs/default.aspx)). I read this as stronger evidence than drug publicity alone. Credit allocation remains a constraint, not a reason to reject the option.

Orexin has the strongest fresh clinical-mechanistic reinforcement. The September 9, 2026 Lasker Basic announcement recognized identification of orexin and the connection between its deficiency and narcolepsy. The FDA approved oveporexton on August 5, 2026, as the first treatment directly targeting the lost orexin signaling underlying narcolepsy type 1 ([Lasker announcement](https://laskerfoundation.org/awards/media-center/), [FDA announcement](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-drug-treat-full-range-narcolepsy-type-1-symptoms)). This makes a compact Nobel narrative: a signaling molecule, a physiological function, a disease mechanism, and a targeted treatment. I give it substantial weight without treating the September award as privileged information about October.

Other contains concrete competition, rather than just an allowance for surprises:

- Optical coherence tomography already received the 2023 Lasker Clinical award. Clarivate's September 17, 2026 Medicine selections recognized it again, alongside immune adhesion receptors and GLP-1 ([OCT Lasker](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/optical-coherence-tomography/), [Clarivate](https://ir.clarivate.com/news-events/press-releases/news-details/2026/Clarivate-Reveals-Citation-Laureates-2026-Recognizing-Transformative-Scientific-Breakthroughs/default.aspx)).
- Nucleic-acid sensing received the Japan Prize announced on January 21, 2026, recognizing Akira and Chen. This adds to Chen's 2024 Lasker for cGAS. The Japan Prize citation is broader than cGAS alone, which limits how narrowly I interpret the signal ([Japan Prize announcement](https://www.japanprize.jp/en/press_releases20260121.html), [Lasker](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/cgas-enzyme-that-senses-self-and-foreign-dna/)).
- Epigenetic regulation and Rett syndrome received the Horwitz recognition announced on September 2, 2026, for Bird and Zoghbi. Taste biology received the 2026 Wolf Medicine prize announced on September 30 ([Columbia: Horwitz](https://www.cuimc.columbia.edu/news/2026-horwitz-prize-awarded-work-epigenetics-neurological-diseases), [Wolf announcement](https://wolffund.org.il/home-page/)).
- Cellular organization through low-complexity protein domains, integrins, and cystic-fibrosis therapy also have major Lasker recognition outside the supplied options ([2025 awards](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/2025-winners/), [2022 awards](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/2022-winners/)).

The remaining named options retain meaningful probability. Optogenetics has transformative methodological importance and a 2021 Lasker. Chaperone-assisted folding and UPR have mature, distinct scientific cores, recognized by Lasker in 2011 and 2014. I do not heavily discount them merely because their precursor awards are older ([optogenetics](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/light-sensitive-microbial-proteins-optogenetics/), [chaperones](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/chaperone-assisted-protein-folding/), [UPR](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/unfolded-protein-response/)).

CAR-T gained further recognition in the BBVA award announcement of February 11, 2026. PCSK9 gained another translational milestone with the FDA's July 17, 2026 approval of the first oral inhibitor. Next-generation sequencing has strong prize standing, but its 2026 Wolf recognition was in Chemistry, making category competition a real discount for this Medicine-only question ([BBVA](https://www.bbva.com/en/frontiers-of-knowledge-award-goes-to-scientists-who-revolutionized-the-treatment-of-several-types-of-blood-cancer/), [FDA](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-oral-pcsk9-inhibitor-lower-ldl-cholesterol-adults-high-cholesterol), [Wolf Chemistry](https://wolffund.org.il/category/field/chemistry/)).

Wnt/organoids, inherited cancer susceptibility, leptin, and anti-TNF remain credible tails. Their recognition establishes importance, but I found less evidence separating their current-year chances from those of the stronger contenders. I also distinguish King's broader Special Achievement award from a dedicated Lasker research award ([Wnt](https://breakthroughprize.org/Laureates/L3792), [King](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/breast-cancer-genetics-and-human-rights/), [leptin](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/leptin-a-hormone-that-regulates-appetite-and-body-weight/), [anti-TNF](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/anti-tnf-for-treating-rheumatoid-arthritis/)).

For the numerical synthesis, I formed an equal-weight linear pool of the supplied discovery-level estimates, then weighted that pool equally with my source-audited assessment. The audited assessment puts more weight on omitted contenders and avoids strong penalties based on topic rotation or the age of a precursor award. Its leading allocations are Other at 35.0%, GLP-1 at 17%, and orexin at 12%; the starting pool puts those at 30.7%, 19%, and 12%, respectively. I calculated every final category as the arithmetic mean of its pooled and audited probabilities and verified that the distribution sums to one. These are judgmental selection probabilities, not fitted statistical coefficients. No market prices, betting odds, or public probability aggregates informed the estimate.

## What's non-obvious

The discovery-matching rule removes much of the apparent uncertainty about the named people. A different GLP-1 or optogenetics laureate combination can still resolve to the listed discovery. Attribution matters because the Nobel permits at most three recipients, but disagreement among precursor-award rosters is not an automatic exclusion ([Nobel statutes](https://www.nobelprize.org/statutes-of-the-nobel-foundation/)). Similarly, the 2024 Chemistry award for protein design and structure prediction did not already reward cellular chaperones or UPR ([official Chemistry motivation](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2024/press-release/)).

The other trap is timing. Clarivate explicitly says its program does not predict Nobel recipients in a specific year. A fresh citation award, a new drug approval, and renewed publicity often reflect the same underlying maturation, so counting them as independent signals exaggerates confidence ([Clarivate's stated scope](https://ir.clarivate.com/news-events/press-releases/news-details/2026/Clarivate-Reveals-Citation-Laureates-2026-Recognizing-Transformative-Scientific-Breakthroughs/default.aspx)). This is why GLP-1 and orexin lead the named field without consuming most of the probability.

## Uncertainties

The largest missing information is the committee's current shortlist and comparative evaluations. I found no verified public disclosure of those records. Their absence is not evidence against any candidate; the selection process is designed to keep them confidential ([Nobel Foundation](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2025/04/annual-review-2024.pdf)). Precursor organizations also share scientific evidence and professional networks, so agreement among assessments does not create independent confirmation.

The final motivation can be narrower or broader than public descriptions of a field. A combined protein-homeostasis award could create a boundary between chaperones and UPR; an organoid award need not match the Wnt option. I retain this wording uncertainty rather than assuming every adjacent discovery qualifies. The decimal places preserve the pooling arithmetic, not empirical knowledge of the committee's preferences to that precision.

## Forecast summary

My highest-probability outcome is **Other (31.5%)**, because the supplied list omits several serious Nobel-ready discoveries. Among the named options, I put **GLP-1 first (15.5%)**, narrowly ahead of **orexin (14.5%)**. Optogenetics, CAR-T, the unfolded protein response, next-generation sequencing, and chaperone-assisted protein folding form the next tier.

The forecast cutoff is **October 2, 2026 at 14:05 UTC**, three days before the scheduled announcement. I found no credible leak or evidence that the result had already become public. Nobel nominations and evaluations remain confidential for 50 years, so public precursor prizes, scientific impact, and attribution patterns are signals of general Nobel-worthiness rather than direct observations of the committee's 2026 choice. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/facts-on-the-nobel-prize-in-physiology-or-medicine/?utm_source=openai))

## Resolution interpretation

I forecast the discovery in the official motivation, not the exact laureates. This matters because several options name a disputable trio, but the resolution criteria say that the people need not match exactly. Attribution complexity still lowers a discovery's probability of being selected—the Nobel can be divided among no more than three people—but it does not prevent an option from resolving YES if the committee recognizes the same discovery using a different laureate combination. Historically, through 2025, Medicine had been awarded 116 times to 232 people; 40 prizes had one laureate, 36 had two, and 40 had three. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-laureates-in-physiology-or-medicine/all/?utm_source=openai))

## Base rates and model

I audited the official Lasker Basic and Clinical award archives for 1990–2025 and matched award groups to later Nobel Medicine prizes by discovery rather than merely by shared recipients. Of 66 Basic/Clinical award groups in the available years, I classified 20, or 30.3%, as later receiving a matching Medicine Nobel by the end of 2025. Only one group, about 1.5%, matched in the same calendar year; under a stricter interpretation even that case is a partial match. Recent Lasker cohorts are heavily right-censored, so 30.3% is not a lifetime ceiling, but the same-year result is an important warning against treating the September 2026 orexin Lasker as quasi-inside information. The Lasker archives and the official Nobel record were the underlying datasets. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/category/awards/?utm_source=openai))

I used a structured qualitative model with five components: approximately 30% weight on transformative importance and breadth, 20% on maturity and validation, 20% on convergence of independent precursor awards, 20% on whether a defensible living laureate set fits within three people, and 10% on fit with the Medicine prize and recent topic history. I then reserved substantial prior probability for omitted discoveries and normalized all mutually exclusive outcomes to 1. Topic rotation received low weight: the recent sequence—peripheral immune tolerance in 2025, microRNA in 2024, mRNA vaccines in 2023, ancient genomes in 2022, and sensory receptors in 2021—provides modest context but no reliable rule. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-laureates-in-physiology-or-medicine/all/?utm_source=openai))

## Leading named options

**GLP-1 — 15.5%.** This has the strongest combination of enormous demonstrated health impact and multi-year award convergence. I nevertheless rank GLP-1 first because the Nobel could use a basic-discovery motivation centered on Mojsov, Holst, and Drucker, which would match this option under the resolution criteria.

**Orexin — 14.5%.** The 2026 Lasker Basic Award explicitly honored Emmanuel Mignot and Masashi Yanagisawa for identifying orexin, establishing its wake-promoting role, and showing that deficiency causes narcolepsy. The discovery is mature, fundamental, medically consequential, and can be explained in one compact causal story. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/2021-winners/?utm_source=openai)) Its main weakness is unusually severe attribution fragmentation: major prizes have variously recognized Deisseroth, Hegemann, Miesenböck, Oesterhelt, Georg Nagel, Edward Boyden, and Ernst Bamberg. Their work uncovered an intracellular quality-control pathway that senses misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum and signals corrective responses; they jointly received the 2014 Lasker, Shaw, and later Breakthrough recognition. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/unfolded-protein-response/?utm_source=openai)) The negatives are the lack of a fresh 2026 catalyst and the possibility that the Nobel views mammalian UPR branches as requiring additional contributors.

## Calibration and uncertainty

This is a high-uncertainty one-off selection with secret deliberations, a large latent candidate pool, and strong dependence on how the Nobel Assembly frames both the discovery and scientific credit. The probabilities therefore reflect broad uncertainty rather than confidence to the displayed decimal places. I did not consult prediction-market prices, betting odds, Metaculus, Manifold, Polymarket, Kalshi, or other public probability aggregates. The values are normalized and sum exactly to 1.0.

## Research approach and decision-relevant questions

I investigated five threads that could materially change the forecast:

1. **Has a listed discovery already received a Nobel, or is there a misleading near-match?**
2. **Which candidates gained meaningful recognition or clinical validation in 2026?**
3. **How predictive are precursor awards, especially a Lasker in the same year?**
4. **Which serious unlisted discoveries require probability in Other?**
5. **Do Chemistry-versus-Medicine category fit, attribution disputes, or resolution wording weaken particular options?**

The evidence came principally from NobelPrize.org, the Nobel historical-data MCP, official Lasker, Breakthrough, Gairdner and Clarivate records, FDA documentation, and institutional scientific commentary. I commissioned an independent precursor-award review and a separate historical Nobel–Lasker audit, then checked their important findings against primary sources. A date-filtered news MCP search provided corroboration rather than the numerical forecast. **No prediction-market prices, betting odds, or public forecast aggregates were used.**

Nobel nominations are confidential for 50 years. Consequently, neither citation recognition nor a public scientist's preference is evidence of an official 2026 shortlist. This institutional opacity is an important reason to retain a broad distribution. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/nomination?trk=public_post_comment-text&utm_source=openai))

I regard the repeated recognition of the same discovery across basic and clinical framings as stronger than publicity surrounding weight-loss drugs alone. However, these awards are correlated judgments of scientific importance, not independent observations of Nobel voting intentions.

Attribution remains a counterweight: the precursor organizations chose different groups. Habener died on **28 December 2025**, according to the scientific society's obituary published **16 March 2026**. His death changes the eligible roster but does not invalidate a discovery-based GLP-1 outcome. Nobel statutes limit a shared award to three people and exclude work by an already-deceased candidate from consideration. ## 5. Explicit numerical model

There is no defensible fitted dataset translating these particular awards into discovery-specific 2026 probabilities. I therefore use a **judgmental evidence-weighting model**, making its subjective inputs explicit.

The baseline column allocates probability according to established scientific merit, precursor recognition and initial Medicine fit. It is an elicited starting distribution, not an observed historical frequency or a claim about an official shortlist. The multiplier captures the net adjustment after considering current-cycle evidence, category competition, attribution and the breadth of unlisted contenders.

| Discovery | Baseline probability | Net multiplier | Unnormalized weight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GLP-1 | 0.120 | 2.40 | 0.28800 |
| Optogenetics | 0.075 | 1.00 | 0.07500 |
| CAR-T | 0.075 | 1.15 | 0.08625 |
| UPR | 0.065 | 1.00 | 0.06500 |
| PCSK9 | 0.035 | 1.10 | 0.03850 |
| NGS | 0.040 | 0.85 | 0.03400 |
| Orexin | 0.065 | 2.80 | 0.18200 |
| Wnt/organoids | 0.035 | 1.00 | 0.03500 |
| Leptin | 0.045 | 1.00 | 0.04500 |
| Anti-TNF | 0.035 | 0.90 | 0.03150 |
| Chaperones | 0.075 | 0.90 | 0.06750 |
| BRCA | 0.045 | 1.15 | 0.05175 |
| Other | 0.290 | 1.60 | 0.46400 |

The baseline probabilities sum to **1.000**. The adjusted weights sum to **1.46350**. For each option, I calculate:

**final probability = baseline probability × net multiplier / 1.46350.**

The largest adjustments are orexin's 2026 Lasker/FDA validation, GLP-1's current recognition layered onto its broad prior record, and the unlisted candidates discovered in the Other investigation. Smaller adjustments deliberately avoid overreacting to weak signals: CAR-T, PCSK9 and BRCA gain modestly; NGS and chaperones face category discounts; anti-TNF lacks a fresh catalyst. These multipliers are **not statistically estimated likelihood ratios**, and correlated awards are incorporated as one net assessment rather than multiplied separately.

I performed the normalization in Python using decimal arithmetic, rounded to six decimal places, and assigned the one-unit rounding residual to Other. The reported probabilities sum to **exactly 1.000000**.

## 6. Sensitivity and remaining uncertainty

To test dependence on the main judgments, I varied the GLP-1 multiplier from **1.8 to 3.2**, orexin from **2.0 to 4.0**, and Other from **1.2 to 2.0**, holding all other inputs fixed and recalculating all eight combinations of endpoints. The resulting ranges were approximately **13.62–27.60% for GLP-1**, **8.01–19.21% for orexin**, and **22.87–39.85% for Other**. These are parameter-sensitivity ranges, not statistical confidence intervals.

The principal unknown is the committee's confidential evaluation, not the public scientific importance of these discoveries. The evidence could also be incomplete: absence of a newly retrieved award is not proof that no relevant recognition exists. Some direct Nobel page requests returned access errors; I used indexed official records and the filtered historical-data MCP rather than treating a failed fetch as a negative result. The Gairdner 2026 webpage also contains an apparent 2025 dateline typo despite its 2026 title and page date; I use its award identities, not that inconsistent dateline, as evidence.

My final judgment is therefore deliberately dispersed: **GLP-1 leads the individual listed discoveries; orexin has the strongest fresh upgrade; Other remains the largest category because substantial unlisted competitors and confidential selection uncertainty cannot reasonably be ignored.**

## Research approach and decision-relevant findings

I examined official Nobel histories and rules, the Lasker Foundation's award records, Clarivate's recognition announcements, Breakthrough, Gairdner and Wolf awards, FDA announcements, and relevant university statements. I supplemented web research with the Nobel and news APIs, a historical crosswalk prepared by a coding researcher, and a specialist review of recent precursor awards. **No prediction-market prices, betting odds, or public forecast aggregates were used in setting the forecast.**

The principal research questions were:

1. **Which candidates have genuinely fresh recognition or clinical validation, rather than merely longstanding prominence?** This strengthened orexin and GLP-1.
2. **How predictive is a recent precursor award of an immediate Nobel?** Historical evidence argues against treating this year's Lasker winner as an overwhelming favorite.
3. **How much important competition is omitted from the options?** Several recent award programs recognize compelling unlisted discoveries, supporting a substantial Other allocation.
4. **Are some candidates more naturally Chemistry discoveries, or already covered by a neighboring Nobel?** This reduces the Medicine-specific sequencing forecast, but does not eliminate chaperone folding or the unfolded protein response.

### GLP-1: strongest named candidate overall

GLP-1 combines foundational physiology, established therapeutic importance and recognition from multiple scientific bodies. The **2024 Lasker Clinical Award** recognized Habener, Mojsov and Knudsen for discovery and development of GLP-1-based obesity treatments. The **2025 Breakthrough Prize** recognized Drucker, Habener, Holst, Knudsen and Mojsov. On **17 September 2026**, Clarivate recognized Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for identifying and characterizing GLP-1 and studying its biological activity. These differently constituted groups reinforce the importance of the discovery-development chain, although I treat their judgments as correlated rather than independent signals. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/glp-1-based-therapy-for-obesity/))

Credit allocation remains a practical complication. Nobel rules permit no more than three individual laureates, whereas the recognition history spans several major contributors. **Joel Habener died on 28 December 2025**, as confirmed by the National Academy of Sciences, and is consequently not a prospective living laureate. His death changes the eligible-person landscape but does not prevent recognition of the discovery through surviving contributors. I apply only a modest credit-allocation discount, particularly because this question does not require the named laureates to match. ([nasonline.org](https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/joel-f-habener-jpqij9/))

My positive assessment is not simply an extrapolation from drug publicity. The Lasker record identifies both the physiologically active hormone and the development of durable medicines, giving the committee a coherent discovery-to-treatment narrative. Conversely, Clarivate explicitly states that its program does **not** aim to predict Nobel recipients in a particular year. Its fresh selection supports scientific standing, not privileged information about Monday's result. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/glp-1-based-therapy-for-obesity/))

## Historical calibration and its limitations

The historical crosswalk covers **2000–2025 inclusive: N = 26 Nobel Medicine prize-years**, using completed official Nobel records and Lasker historical award-year records available at the cutoff. The unit is a prize-year, not a person. A positive requires a corresponding Nobel contributor to have received a Lasker **Basic or Clinical** award by that Nobel year; Public Service and Special Achievement awards are excluded. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-laureates-in-physiology-or-medicine/all/?utm_source=openai))

The audit establishes **17/26 positive years, or 65.3846%**, and **10/16, or 62.5%, for 2010–2025**. Selected corresponding Nobel-year/Lasker-year pairs are: 2000/1983, 2001/1998, 2003/1984, 2005/1995, 2007/2001, 2008/1986, 2009/2006, 2010/2001, 2011/2007, 2012/2009, 2013/2013, 2015/2011, 2018/2015, 2019/2016, 2020/2000, 2023/2021 and 2024/2008. These pairs permit reproduction of the arithmetic from the two official archives. ([nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-laureates-in-physiology-or-medicine/all/?utm_source=openai))

Among these established matches, **seven** have a calendar-year lag of 0–3 years: **7/26 = 26.9231%** of all prize-years. Only **one established same-year match**, Südhof in 2013, appears: **1/26 = 3.8462%**. The selected matched lags have a **four-year median**. These calculations support recognition as a useful signal without implying that the newest Lasker winner is usually the immediate Nobel winner. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/2013-winners/))

There are important qualifications. Unmatched rows are not exhaustively verified negative records, so the positive counts are lower bounds. Some matches concern only one component of a divided Nobel, whereas this question selects only the larger-share or first-mentioned discovery. Kandel's learning/memory match is also broader than the Nobel's signal-transduction wording. Most importantly, **P(previous Lasker | Nobel winner) is not P(this year's Nobel | Lasker winner)**. I use this small historical sample to restrain overconfidence, not to estimate a fitted annual winning probability. I likewise do not use the present list's retrospective failure to match past Nobel discoveries as a base rate for Other: the list was selected from currently unrewarded contenders.

## Reproducible probability construction

I combine two assessment lenses:

- **A: fundamental discovery, maturity and breadth**, emphasizing durable scientific importance.
- **T: therapeutic validation and timely recognition**, emphasizing established medical benefit and recent corroborating evidence.

The following scores are **subjective relative selection weights**, not citation counts, measurements, or statistically fitted coefficients. They encode the comparative assessments above. Other is an aggregate of omitted candidates and therefore receives a larger score than most individual discoveries.

| Discovery | A score | T score |
|---|---:|---:|
| GLP-1 | 210 | 480 |
| Optogenetics | 120 | 20 |
| CAR-T | 45 | 100 |
| Unfolded protein response | 100 | 35 |
| PCSK9 | 30 | 85 |
| Next-generation sequencing | 40 | 30 |
| Orexin | 100 | 220 |
| Wnt/organoids | 40 | 15 |
| Leptin | 35 | 15 |
| TNF-targeted therapy | 15 | 35 |
| Chaperone-mediated folding | 120 | 25 |
| Inherited breast/ovarian susceptibility | 40 | 20 |
| Other | 420 | 290 |
| **Total** | **1315** | **1370** |

I normalize each column and combine them using:

**p(i) = 0.60 × A(i)/1315 + 0.40 × T(i)/1370.**

The 60/40 weighting is a judgmental robustness choice, not a claim that precisely 60% of Nobel selections belong to a distinct fundamental category. For GLP-1, for example, the calculation is **0.60 × 210/1315 + 0.40 × 480/1370 = 0.235963475…**. Python was used to normalize the scores, calculate every probability and verify the total.

Relative to my first independent assessment, additional primary-source checks increased orexin from approximately **7.67% to 10.99%**, increased GLP-1 from **21.82% to 23.60%**, and increased sequencing from **1.98% to 2.70%**. These were evidence-based revisions, principally reflecting orexin's fresh award and FDA milestone, GLP-1's clarified recognition/eligible-contributor landscape, and sequencing's fresh Wolf recognition—not movement toward market prices.

As a sensitivity check, varying the fundamental-lens weight from **40% to 80%**, while holding the score columns fixed, gives GLP-1 approximately **19.78–27.41%**, orexin **9.30–12.68%**, and Other **25.48–29.78%**. These are model-sensitivity ranges, not statistical confidence intervals; uncertainty about the relative scores and hidden committee preferences is wider.

**Bottom line:** GLP-1 has the strongest overall named case, orexin deserves a substantial upward adjustment for unusually timely validation, and the unlisted field remains too strong to concentrate most probability on either. The six decimal places in the output preserve the calculation; they do not imply knowledge of committee preferences to millionth-level accuracy. Other is adjusted by the tiny rounding residual so that the reported probabilities sum exactly to 1.

This is a substantial unlisted genetics/neuroscience discovery family. ([cuimc.columbia.edu](https://www.cuimc.columbia.edu/news/2026-horwitz-prize-awarded-work-epigenetics-neurological-diseases))
- **cGAS DNA sensing:** Chen's **2024 Lasker Basic award** supplies a strong unlisted immune-sensing candidate. cGAS is not anti-TNF therapy or CAR-T. ([laskerfoundation.org](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/cgas-enzyme-that-senses-self-and-foreign-dna/?utm_source=openai))
- **Acute promyelocytic leukemia mechanisms and targeted treatment:** the **2026 Shaw award**, documented by the French Academy of Sciences on **May 27, 2026**, recognized Dejean, de Thé and Chen. This is cancer treatment, but not CAR-T. ([academie-sciences.fr](https://www.academie-sciences.fr/anne-dejean-hugues-de-et-zhu-chen-recoivent-shaw-prize?utm_source=openai))
- **Other disease mechanisms and therapeutic discoveries:** the **April 18, 2026 Breakthrough announcement** recognized inherited retinal gene therapy, fetal-to-adult hemoglobin switching and ALS/frontotemporal-dementia genetics. The **April 5, 2025 announcement** also recognized multiple-sclerosis research and DNA-editing developments. These expand the credible competing pool, although I do not regard all of them as equally likely Medicine Nobel winners. ([breakthroughprize.org](https://breakthroughprize.org/News/98))
- **Cellular organization:** phase separation received the **2023 Breakthrough Prize**, and the Lasker archive records low-complexity protein domains and cystic-fibrosis treatment among its **2025** discoveries. These are additional omitted routes to recognition. ([breakthroughprize.org](https://breakthroughprize.org/News/73))

The aggregation matters: Other can be more probable than any single named discovery without any single omitted discovery being my favorite. My initial independent allocation to Other was 30%; corroborating the breadth of the omitted pool led me to raise it to **32%**. This update was based on specific scientific-award evidence, not a market signal.

## 5. Reproducible probability construction

There is insufficient public information to fit a reliable model of this year's private committee deliberations. I therefore use an equal-weight mixture of **two explicitly judgmental scenarios**, not a purportedly estimated statistical model:

- **Scenario A:** greater emphasis on recent medical translation and current recognition. It assigns **26% to Other** and 74% to the listed discoveries.
- **Scenario B:** broader emphasis on mature fundamental mechanisms, with less confidence that this list captures the winning discovery. It assigns **38% to Other** and 62% to the listed discoveries.

Within each scenario, the following conditional weights distribute the probability allocated to the twelve named discoveries. Each column sums to 100. These weights are my synthesis of the evidence above, not empirical frequencies or externally supplied forecasts.

| Discovery | A conditional weight, % | B conditional weight, % |
|---|---:|---:|
| GLP-1 | 27 | 17 |
| Optogenetics | 7 | 12 |
| CAR-T | 10 | 8 |
| Unfolded protein response | 6 | 12 |
| PCSK9 | 5 | 6 |
| Next-generation sequencing | 4 | 6 |
| Orexin | 20 | 11 |
| Wnt/organoids | 4 | 4 |
| Leptin | 3 | 3 |
| Anti-TNF | 3 | 2 |
| Chaperone-mediated folding | 7 | 14 |
| Inherited breast/ovarian susceptibility | 4 | 5 |

For a named discovery i, the final calculation is:

**P(i) = 0.5 × [0.74 × A_i/100 + 0.62 × B_i/100].**

For Other:

**P(Other) = 0.5 × (0.26 + 0.38) = 0.32.**

For example, GLP-1 is 0.5 × (0.74 × 0.27 + 0.62 × 0.17) = **0.1526**. Orexin is 0.5 × (0.74 × 0.20 + 0.62 × 0.11) = **0.1081**. I performed the calculations in Python using decimal arithmetic and verified that all probabilities are between zero and one and sum to **exactly 1.00000**.

## 6. Uncertainty and data-quality safeguards

The main uncertainty is unobserved committee preference, not whether these discoveries are important. Recent awards are correlated indicators, so I do not multiply them as independent likelihood ratios. I also distinguish an award's designated year from its announcement date: for example, the 2023 orexin Breakthrough was announced in September 2022. Website modification timestamps likewise are not discovery dates or original announcement dates. ([breakthroughprize.org](https://breakthroughprize.org/News/73))

As a sensitivity check, changing Scenario A's mixture weight from 25% to 75%, while retaining the scenario inputs, moves Other from **35% to 29%**, GLP-1 from **12.9% to 17.62%**, and orexin from **8.815% to 12.805%**. These are calculated scenario sensitivities, not confidence intervals. Additional uncertainty about the hidden selection process and omitted candidates is larger than this simple test captures.

The reported decimal places preserve the arithmetic of the stated model. They should **not** be interpreted as evidence that Nobel selection probabilities are known to basis-point accuracy. My final distribution deliberately keeps substantial probability across competing discoveries and a broad Other category.

Individual coverage windows and work sample sizes are retained in the [profile data and calculation](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md). I accept these premises without a vintage or attribution penalty. Cohort percentiles and foundation shares are fractions; inventions, patents and books are counts ([supplied definitions](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)).

The unlisted pool has substantial depth. Optical coherence tomography received the 2023 clinical Lasker, and integrin biology received the 2022 basic Lasker ([OCT](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/optical-coherence-tomography/); [integrins](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/integrins-mediators-of-cell-matrix-cell-adhesion/)). Clarivate's September 17, 2026 Medicine selections included both these unlisted families alongside GLP-1 ([official release](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-reveals-citation-laureates-2026-recognizing-transformative-scientific-breakthroughs/)). Other credible omissions include cGAS DNA sensing, TOR nutrient sensing and low-complexity protein domains, each with discovery-specific Lasker recognition ([cGAS](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/cgas-enzyme-that-senses-self-and-foreign-dna/); [TOR](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/nutrient-activated-tor-proteins-that-regulate-cell-growth/); [low-complexity domains](https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/structures-and-functions-of-low-complexity-domains/)). The April 18, 2026 Breakthrough awards add distinct gene-replacement and fetal-hemoglobin-regulation routes ([official announcement](https://breakthroughprize.org/News/98)). I assign Other 40.0% as a coverage judgment, not an observed shortlist-miss rate ([calculation](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)).

For named discoveries, the balanced career score gives impact, translation, textbook reach and collaboration weights of 40%, 30%, 25% and 5%. It combines the strongest person's score with the group mean in a 65:35 ratio. Career evidence receives 80% of the combined score; matching defining works receive 20%, emphasizing foundation share over disruption. Shared papers are counted once. Relative weights are proportional to the exponential of five times the combined score ([full formulas and inputs](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)).

Rather than commit to one set of coefficients, I average 81 specifications varying career weights, strongest-person aggregation, defining-work weight and exponential scale. The balanced perspective receives most of the ensemble weight. A 10% uniform component accounts for committee priorities absent from the profiles. The strongest fresh secondary signal belongs to orexin. I increase each discovery's relative profile weight by 35%, then renormalize. Sequencing receives a small 10% category discount because the earlier sequencing Nobel went to Chemistry in 1980; this is a Medicine-fit judgment, not an eligibility exclusion ([historical award](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1980/press-release/1000/); [adjustment calculation](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)). All other secondary multipliers are neutral ([adjustments](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)).

## What's non-obvious

An outstanding career is not the same thing as outstanding evidence for the resolving discovery. Stratton's BRAF paper does not directly support BRCA susceptibility, Seidah's coronavirus papers do not establish PCSK9, and Rosenberg's broader immunotherapy record is not itself a CAR-T defining paper. Their career profiles still contribute, but the discovery-specific component excludes unrelated work. This prevents a spectacular result in a neighboring field from driving the wrong option ([selected works and scoring rules](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)).

Recent recognition establishes scientific standing, not the committee's choice this year. Clarivate explicitly says its program does not predict recipients in a particular year ([program disclaimer](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-reveals-citation-laureates-2026-recognizing-transformative-scientific-breakthroughs/)). Nor can this slate's coverage be estimated by counting how many already-awarded historical discoveries it omits: that comparison selects against a list of discoveries still awaiting recognition. I use concrete unlisted alternatives to set Other, and keep recent awards secondary when ranking the named options ([coverage reasoning](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)).

## Uncertainties

The largest gap is the committee's undisclosed shortlist and priorities. Nobel nomination information remains confidential for 50 years, so these are not probabilities derived from verified current nominees ([official archive rules](https://www.nobelprize.org/nomination/archive/)). Comparable profiles for the strongest omitted discoveries would sharpen the residual allocation. Official wording also matters: a broad stem-cell award does not automatically match Wnt/organoids, and protein-stress signaling must not be collapsed into chaperone-assisted folding ([resolution boundaries](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)).

At a fixed 40.0% for Other, the scoring variants put both optogenetics and Wnt/organoids between 6% and 11%. I regard 30%–50.0% as a reasonable sensitivity range for Other; that rescales the named probabilities. These are judgmental model ranges, not statistical confidence intervals. The decimal precision in the probability object preserves the calculation, not certainty about the committee's decision ([sensitivity results](sandbox:/mnt/data/nobel_2026_profile_model.md)).
